Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

vignette: Samir Hassan spent thirty-two years working rooftops across the Midwest, but the incident at a decommissioned chemical processing plant still anchored his days. He was thirty-eight, scraping toxic industrial sealant from a corroded ventilation shaft when a pressurized valve burst, flooding the confined attic with acrid, yellow vapor. He remembered the metallic burn in his lungs, the way his three crewmates collapsed against the rafters, and the long, shuddering gasp as the emergency extractors finally cleared the air. The hospital treated his acute pulmonary damage, but the physical wounds healed faster than the dread that settled into his nervous system. Decades later, while perched on the sloped asphalt of a municipal building, scraping away decades of cracked shingles, Samir watched a group of neighborhood children chase a ball across the gravel lot below. The sight of children playing near his work site did not merely remind him of his past; it actively cracked open the sealed vault of his memory, pulling the raw, unbidden recollections of that attic back into his awareness. The sudden return of those fragmented recollections kept his body in a state of perpetual emergency. Whenever the past forced its way into his thoughts, often carrying only the suffocating emotional weight of the spill without a clear image, his heart would hammer and his muscles would lock. The uncontrolled access to that terror meant he stopped recognizing safety. His nervous system remained permanently wound tight, unable to ease his shoulders even in his own bed, and he spent countless nights staring at the ceiling, certain the air was still thick with poison. This unyielding hyperarousal did not just follow his distress; it became the engine of his daily existence, leaving him chronically unable to relax and trapped in a physical state of sustained alarm. This resurfaced psychological weight altered his perception of his surroundings. Every time the trauma intruded, his mind automatically began scanning his environment for matching threats, transforming familiar voices and broadcast reports into sources of acute alarm. The memories did not just occupy his thoughts; they actively recruited the triggers, making every known face from his old crew and every news segment feel like a direct precursor to disaster. Samir had come to believe that proximity to vulnerable groups or the mention of industrial safety meant another collapse was inevitable, so he systematically avoided the evening news and stopped answering calls from his former site managers. The memories did not merely haunt him; they actively manufactured the very stimuli he now fought to escape. His persistent physiological state ensured that these external stimuli held his attention. Because he could not relax even in safe spaces, his nervous system remained permanently calibrated to danger. The chronic startle response and the unyielding inability to unwind did not merely follow his anxiety; they actively magnified his reactions to the media and the people around him, making routine encounters feel explosively threatening. When his wife reached to adjust his collar over breakfast, his body would jolt as if struck, and the constant physiological alarm actively magnified his sensitivity to his coworkers’ familiar voices, turning every known person into a perceived hazard. The threat system did not just amplify the triggers; it dictated their frequency and intensity, ensuring his daily routine remained a minefield of anticipated harm. Over months, the avoidance deepened his isolation, and the insomnia eroded his marriage until he began sleeping in a recliner in the den to stop his wife from jolting awake when he gasped in his sleep. At seventy-eight, Samir finally scheduled an appointment not because he wanted to revisit the attic, but because he was desperate to silence the alarms before his heart gave out, hoping someone could show him how to stop waiting for the next spill.
